newsitem.title: FRANCE: Giscard revives EMU debate at dangerous time.
newsitem.headline: Giscard revives EMU debate at dangerous time.

text.p: Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing could hardly have chosen a more sensitive time to revive debate in France on European monetary union.

The government is deeply unpopular, people are increasingly inclined to blame mass unemployment on the drive to a single currency, and conservative members of parliament are getting anxious about losing their seats in elections due in 1998.
But possibly more important, economists say, it comes at a time when the government itself is at odds with Germany over key elements of policy in fulfilling the single currency dream.
"Apparently there are big tensions between France and Germany about exchange rate policy for the euro and about the stability pact," ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard said.
Giscard d'Estaing called in a magazine article on Wednesday for a sharp depreciation in the franc against the dollar and criticised a decade-old policy of linking the franc to the mark.
His call -- and its revival of the debate about the whole drive to Economic and Monetary Union -- risks drawing attention to those Franco-German policy differences in coming weeks.
On exchange rate policy, France's insistence that the dollar is undervalued against European currencies has found little real echo in Germany.
"I believe that France and Germany have somewhat different views on the subject," said Bernard Godement, economist at Daiwa Institute of Research.

It was in Germany's interest to have a strong yen since its main competitor was Japan, while France wanted a strong dollar because French industry competed with U.S. companies. "A strong dollar is not especially conducive to a strong yen," he said.
France is also at odds with Germany over the planned budget stability pact meant to ensure monetary union members do not run up big budget deficits after the single currency starts in 1999.

While Germany is insisting on a numerical definition of the exceptional circumstances which could exempt countries from paying fines under the pact, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said last week it would be very unwise to fix a figure.
Germany's insistence on getting its own way on the stability pact has been taken badly in some political circles here and some politicians have nicknamed it an "austerity pact".
France and Germany put on a united front on Thursday by issuing a joint statement repeating their commitment to EMU and saying the current franc-mark rate reflected fundamentals.
A source in Prime Minister Alain Juppe's office said the statement came from concern in both Paris and Bonn that Giscard d'Estaing's call for a lower franc was unsettling.

But unlike the days when late French president Francois Mitterrand and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl could brush aside most obstacles in the drive to EMU, the government is now widely seen to be in disarray and reshuffle rumours are rife.

Unemployment is at a record 12.6 percent and according to a recent report prepared for the French Senate, growth is likely to remain too weak to stop a rising trend in joblessness, heaping the worries on jittery politicians.

The renewed French debate on Europe also coincides with a drive by Europe's Mediterranean members -- Italy, Spain and Portugal -- to make sure they join EMU when it is first launched in 1999, fuelling other worries about the single currency.

Germany in particular is anxious that Italian membership of EMU could weaken the new euro, while France would not like to see the future European Central Bank respond by pushing up interest rates to defend the currency, economists say.
That would mean Europe starting out on a single currency with tight monetary policies, ongoing public spending cuts to cut budget deficits and high levels of unemployment.
France also wants to make sure that Italy is not allowed to lock in a low level for lira when it rejoins the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), expected by many this weekend.
Its officials have often attacked the lira's sharp fall after it left the ERM in 1992 as a competitive devaluation which boosted Italy's textile industry and the expense of France's.
For some economists, the public debate this week in France about the strong franc may partly have been a reflection of a private debate about the franc's level against the lira.
A senior source said in Frankfurt on Friday that Europe's monetary committee was due to meet this weekend to discuss the lira's re-entry to the ERM.
